metadata.title: Precision vs Recall: Why Accuracy Can Mislead You — Short
metadata.factual_scope: Portrait-native classification-metric explainer using one explicitly hypothetical transaction example.
metadata.methodological_boundary: Accuracy remains useful; precision, recall, F1, and threshold choices depend on the decision context and the costs of different errors.
metadata.production_gate: Direct clean-master production authorized; no separate review or slate export.

beats.narration_text: Hi, my name is Ushasvi Rachel, and this video is about precision, recall, and why accuracy alone can be misleading in machine learning. A model can look highly accurate while failing on the small group we care about most.

shot.visual_intent: Integrated presenter introduction and minority-class hook.

beats.narration_text: Here is a hypothetical example. Imagine one thousand transactions: nine hundred ninety are normal, and ten are fraudulent. Predicting normal every time gives ninety-nine percent accuracy, but detects zero fraud. The accuracy is mathematically correct, yet incomplete for this decision.

A confusion matrix separates four outcomes. A true positive correctly finds a positive case. A false positive is a false alarm. A false negative misses a real positive. And a true negative correctly finds a negative case. These categories show what accuracy can hide.

shot.visual_intent: Large vertical confusion matrix with all four outcomes.

beats.narration_text: Precision asks: of everything predicted as positive, how many were actually positive? Conceptually, that is true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. Precision describes the reliability of positive predictions.

Precision matters when false alarms are costly. In fraud detection, incorrectly flagging legitimate transactions can block users unnecessarily. That does not make precision universally more important; it means the cost of false positives matters in this setting.

Recall asks: of all actual positive cases, how many did the model find? Conceptually, that is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. Recall describes coverage of the positive class.

Recall matters when missing a positive case is costly. In our hypothetical fraud setting, an undetected fraudulent transaction may be more damaging than investigating some extra alerts. Again, context decides; recall is not always the priority.

Changing a classification threshold can affect precision and recall. One setting may find more positives; another may reduce false alarms. But this is not always a fixed one-for-one tradeoff. The behavior depends on the model and data.

shot.visual_intent: Vertical threshold control and qualified metric comparison.

beats.narration_text: F1 combines precision and recall using their harmonic mean. It can be useful when both matter, but it is not automatically the best metric. Accuracy is not useless either. Choose evaluation metrics by asking which real-world mistake carries the greatest cost.

shot.visual_intent: F1 boundary and error-cost decision visual.

beats.narration_text: The useful question is not only, how often is the model correct? Ask how reliable its positive predictions are, how many real positives it finds, and which errors matter. Accuracy tells you how often the model is right. Precision and recall tell you what kinds of mistakes it is making.

shot.visual_intent: Final metric summary and exact approved takeaway.
